title: Tell me about a time you delivered under an aggressive deadline
prompt: Tell me about a time you had to deliver something important under an aggressive, non-negotiable deadline. How did you make it work, and what tradeoffs did you have to make?
blurb: Tight deadline: did they prioritize and make smart, honest tradeoffs — or just heroics and hidden debt?

rubric.label: Situation & the deadline
rubric.description: Clearly frames the deliverable, why the deadline was real and tight, and what was at stake if they missed.

rubric.label: Owning delivery
rubric.description: Shows they took charge of making the date achievable — not just grinding, but shaping scope, plan, and expectations.

rubric.label: Prioritization & tradeoffs
rubric.description: Describes the concrete tradeoffs THEY made — what to cut, defer, parallelize, or simplify — and the reasoning, rather than 'we just worked harder'.

rubric.label: Result & impact
rubric.description: States whether they hit the date and the outcome, quantified, including quality and any debt incurred.

rubric.label: Reflection & sustainability
rubric.description: Reflects on managing tradeoffs and stakeholders honestly, the cost of the crunch (debt, team burnout), and how they'd avoid repeat fire-drills.

rubric.label: Communication & stakeholder management
rubric.description: Shows they set expectations and communicated tradeoffs/risk to stakeholders, and tells the story clearly.

reference.scenario: The candidate should recall a real crunch — a launch tied to an event, a customer commitment, a compliance date, a competitive window — with a deadline they couldn't move. The signal is smart prioritization and honest tradeoff-making (and stakeholder communication), not sustained heroics or hiding corners cut. The best answers show they shaped scope and expectations, not just effort.
model_points: Situation: a genuinely tight, meaningful deadline with clear stakes for missing it.
Task: they owned hitting it and quickly assessed what was actually required versus nice-to-have.
Action: made explicit tradeoffs — ruthlessly cut/deferred scope to the true must-haves, simplified, parallelized work, unblocked dependencies, and pulled in help where it mattered.
Action: communicated proactively — set expectations with stakeholders on what would and wouldn't be in v1, surfaced risk early rather than promising everything and failing late.
Result: hit the date (or a renegotiated one) with the core value intact; quantified outcome; honest about any tech debt or deferred scope and the plan to pay it down.
Reflection: recognizes crunch as a tool, not a lifestyle; reflects on team sustainability and on preventing the next avoidable fire-drill (earlier planning, better estimates, saying no sooner).

probes.question: Beyond working harder, what did you decide NOT to do? Walk me through the specific tradeoffs and how you chose them.
If nothing was cut and the deadline was truly aggressive, either the scope was small or something gave — what actually gave? Quality? Debt?
How did you set expectations with whoever was waiting on this? Did they know what was being deferred?
What corners did you cut, and what happened to that debt afterward — did it get paid down or bite you?
Was this avoidable? What would have prevented the crunch in the first place?

red_flags: The whole answer is heroics — nights and weekends — with no prioritization or scoping.
Cut corners silently and left hidden debt or quality problems without acknowledging it.
Over-promised to stakeholders and there's no honest account of what slipped.
Burned out the team and shows no awareness of the human cost or sustainability.
No tradeoff reasoning — 'we did it all somehow' — or claims a truly tight deadline was hit with full scope and no cost.
Blames others (unrealistic manager, slow teammates) with no ownership of the plan.
follow_ups: How did you decide what was a true must-have versus a nice-to-have?
How did you keep quality acceptable while moving fast — what did you refuse to compromise on?
What happened to the deferred scope and any debt afterward?
How did you protect the team from burning out, and would you take this deadline again?
reference.exemplar_answer: Situation: 'We committed to launching a new checkout flow before a major sales event six weeks out — the date was fixed by marketing spend and couldn't move. Our original plan was ten weeks of work.' Task: 'I owned delivery and had to close a four-week gap without slipping the date.' Action: 'Instead of just adding hours, I re-cut the scope. I listed every planned feature and sorted by whether it was required to safely take money on the new flow. Three items — saved cards, a redesigned promo UI, and A/B infra — were valuable but not required for launch, so I deferred them and said so explicitly to the PM and marketing, in writing, with the risk laid out. I parallelized the payment integration and the UI by agreeing on the API contract up front, and I brought in one extra engineer for the critical path only. The one thing I refused to compromise was payment-correctness testing.' Result: 'We shipped the core flow two days before the event; it handled the traffic with zero payment defects and drove roughly $X in event sales. The three deferred items shipped over the following month as planned.' Reflection: 'The lesson was that under a hard date, scope is the lever, not effort — and that saying clearly what you're NOT doing is what keeps trust when you deliver less than the original wish-list. It was also a near-avoidable fire-drill; we've since started pressure-testing timelines against the calendar earlier so commitments are realistic from the start.'

interviewer_notes: The signal is prioritization and honest tradeoffs, not endurance. If the answer is all heroics, probe 'what did you decide NOT to do'. If they claim full scope on a truly tight deadline, something gave — press on quality or hidden debt. Always check stakeholder communication: did whoever was waiting know what was being deferred, or were they surprised? Reward candor about debt and a plan to pay it down; penalize silent corner-cutting. Senior-ish maturity shows in acknowledging the human cost and in preventing the next avoidable crunch. Probe I-vs-we on who made the scoping calls.
